old_content:
It starts with a conversation about where you need help and what you want to stay the same. If you’d like to take the next step, we’ll arrange a free visit at home. We’ll agree a care plan with you and introduce you to your carers before your care begins.

1. The first conversation

You speak to someone in our Maidstone office, not a call centre. We will ask what is happening, what a normal day looks like now, and what has changed. This first call is free and takes about twenty minutes. There is nothing to sign and no visit booked at the end of it unless you want one.

If we are not the right fit, perhaps because you need a nursing home or live outside our area, we will explain why and point you towards a more suitable service.

2. The assessment visit

A senior member of our team comes to you, usually within a few days. It is a conversation in your front room, and the visit is free. We look at the practical things (stairs, bathroom, medication, mealtimes, who else is involved) and the things that matter just as much: what time you like to get up, which programmes you would rather not miss, whether you want company or would prefer someone to get on quietly.

Family are welcome to be there. So is a social worker, district nurse or case manager if one is already involved. If care is being arranged after a hospital stay, we will work to the discharge date rather than our own diary.

3. Your care plan

We write the plan with you, and you keep a copy in your home. It sets out what happens at each visit, in what order, and what to do when things do not go to plan: who to call, what your preferences are, which medication needs prompting rather than administering.

The plan also records your everyday preferences: how you like your tea, which door to use and what you prefer to be called. These details help each carer support you in the way you want.

4. Meeting your care team

You are matched with a small named team (usually two to four carers) chosen for the shifts you need and, where we can, for who is likely to get on with you. You meet them before they start. If you do not feel comfortable with someone, please tell us so we can arrange a different match.

A small team means a carer will notice that you are quieter than usual, or that the fridge is fuller than it should be: the kind of early sign that only shows up to someone who was there last week too.

5. The first week

A senior carer works alongside the team for the first visits, so the handover happens in person. Together, we check that the timings, tasks and routines work for you, and make any adjustments needed.

We call you at the end of the first week to ask what is working and what is not.

6. Keeping in touch

Every visit is logged, and family members who you have agreed can see them are able to. If a carer has a concern (a new bruise, a missed meal, a change in mood), it is raised the same day.

We review the plan formally after six weeks and then at least every six months, and any time your needs change. If you go into hospital, we will keep in contact with the ward so that coming home does not mean starting again from scratch.

If something changes suddenly

Care needs rarely change on a schedule. If you need more support quickly (after a fall, an infection, or a change in medication), call the office and we will look at it that day. Out of hours there is always someone on call, and they have access to your plan. This is not an emergency service: in a medical emergency, call 999.

Safeguarding and raising a concern

Every carer is DBS-checked, trained in safeguarding before their first shift, and works to a code of conduct we will show you on request. If you are ever unhappy with something, tell the office. You will get a named person, a timescale, and an answer in writing. Concerns about someone’s safety are acted on immediately and, where required, reported to the local authority and the Care Quality Commission.

You can read the CQC’s own assessment of us on our CQC and our care page.

Paying for care

Some people fund their own care, some receive funding from Kent County Council, and some are funded through NHS Continuing Healthcare. We will tell you honestly which is likely to apply and what the process involves, including where you may be entitled to an assessment you have not been offered. Our rates and what they include are set out in the common questions.

When you are ready

There is no obligation at any point before care starts, and no notice period to agree in advance. If you would like to talk it through, send us a message or call the office. A conversation costs you nothing and usually makes the next step clearer.
